name: Stacked Generalization Model
analogy: Think of it as a trading desk with three analysts and a head of desk. Each analyst gives a probability of the next move, and the head of desk has learned from past calls how much to trust each analyst, so the final call is a weighted blend rather than a plain average.

steps.title: Pick different kinds of base models
steps.description: You choose several first-level models that think in different ways, for example a tree-based model, a nearest-neighbour model and a simple linear model. They are chosen to disagree in useful ways, because three copies of the same idea add nothing.
steps.inExample: Three base models are chosen: a boosted-tree model, a nearest-neighbour model and a logistic model, all fed the same 5-minute MNQ bar features.

steps.title: Collect honest out-of-sample guesses
steps.description: The training bars are cut into blocks. Each base model learns on all blocks but one and then guesses the held-out block. Repeating this gives every training bar a guess made by a model that never saw that bar, which stops the next level from learning from flattering, memorised answers.
steps.inExample: For each of 40,000 training bars, each base model produces a probability of closing higher 6 bars later, always from a block it was not trained on.

steps.title: Build a table of the guesses
steps.description: These honest guesses become a new, small table: one row per bar, one column per base model, plus the true outcome. This table is the only thing the second-level model will ever see.
steps.inExample: The table has 40,000 rows and 3 columns of probabilities, next to a column showing whether the close really was higher.

steps.title: Train the head of desk on the table
steps.description: A deliberately simple second-level model learns how to combine the columns: which base model to lean on, which to discount, and whether one analyst is consistently too confident. Keeping it simple matters because it has few columns and could overfit easily.
steps.inExample: The second-level model learns to give the boosted-tree model half the say, the logistic model three tenths and the nearest-neighbour model two tenths.

steps.title: Retrain the base models on everything
steps.description: Once the combining rule is known, each base model is trained again on the full training data so that it is as informed as possible when it faces new bars.
steps.inExample: All three base models are refit on the full 40,000 training bars before the live bar arrives.

steps.title: Score a new bar in two layers
steps.description: A new bar goes to every base model first. Their three guesses are then handed to the head of desk, which applies the learned blend and returns one final probability.
steps.inExample: The 14:35 bar gets 58, 52 and 55 percent from the three analysts, and the blend returns about 56 percent.

useFor.task: Getting more from several decent models
useFor.example: You already have a boosted-tree model and a linear model for MNQ direction, and you want one probability that uses both rather than choosing one.

useFor.task: Combining models that look at different information
useFor.example: Blending a model built on price indicators with one built on FinBERT news sentiment, so the blend can lean on news only when it has historically helped.

useFor.task: Reducing the risk of betting on one model
useFor.example: A single model can have a bad fold; a blend of several is often steadier from one walk-forward fold to the next.

useFor.task: Final stage of a research pipeline
useFor.example: After testing many separate models on the same folds, stacking the best few into one signal that the cost-aware backtest then judges.

avoidWhen: You have little data; the honest-guess step cuts the data into blocks and the second level adds another thing to fit, so a single simple model is safer.
Time order matters inside the data; ordinary random blocks leak the future into the table of guesses, so the blocks must be time-ordered with a gap, which makes stacking slower and fiddlier.
You need to explain every call in one sentence; a two-layer blend is harder to describe than one model.

example.scenario: A 5-minute MNQ bar closes at 14:35. Three base models each give a probability that the close 6 bars (30 minutes) later will be above this close, and a second-level model blends them into one probability.

input.summary: The three base-model probabilities for this bar, plus the weights the second-level model learned from past honest guesses.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The price at which the 14:35 five-minute bar closed.

fields.name: boosted-tree probability of a higher close
fields.meaning: The first base model's guess that the close 6 bars later will be higher.

fields.name: nearest-neighbour probability of a higher close
fields.meaning: The second base model's guess, based on how similar past bars turned out.

fields.name: logistic probability of a higher close
fields.meaning: The third base model's guess from a simple weighted sum of features.

fields.name: learned weight on the boosted-tree model
fields.meaning: How much of the final answer comes from the boosted-tree model.

fields.name: learned weight on the logistic model
fields.meaning: How much of the final answer comes from the logistic model.

fields.name: learned weight on the nearest-neighbour model
fields.meaning: How much of the final answer comes from the nearest-neighbour model.

output.summary: One blended probability and the side it points to.

fields.name: blended probability of a higher close
fields.meaning: Half of 58, plus 30 percent of 55, plus 20 percent of 52, which comes to about 56 percent.

fields.name: call
fields.meaning: The side the probability falls on when the dividing line is 50 percent.

fields.name: largest contributor
fields.meaning: The base model that carried the most weight in this bar's final answer.

example.reading: 56 percent is a small lean, a little under the strongest single analyst. That is typical: blending trims the extremes. Whether it earns anything depends on trading costs, which the run page's net result measures on held-out folds.
